subsystem.name: messagebus
subsystem.note: The S8 durable-messaging belt, interlock tests/messagebus, 5 files. One ledger per source file (D-0019). The belt's whole design constraint is that it adds NO delivery store: interlock's own bus.py opens by defining itself as a thin facade that uses the S7 outbox API as found, so send / recipient-filtered poll / ack / envelope / endpoint is the entire owned surface and retry counting, delivery state transitions, lease fencing, destination dedup and ack persistence all stay in src/control_plane/outbox.ts. The single xfailed case in the whole 2,199-case source baseline lives in this belt (tests/messagebus/test_carried_specifications.py's recipient-aliasing specification).

file.note: interlock's item 6 acceptance core, and the durable half of interlock Issue #19 together with the import-graph assertion beside it. systematic_mappings.from: `bus.send(message_id=..., recipient=..., payload=..., dedup_key=..., now_ms=..., epoch=..., run_id=...)`, `bus.poll(recipient, now_ms=..., epoch=..., clock=...)`, `bus.ack(message_id, now_ms=..., recipient=...)` -- Python keyword arguments in snake_case
systematic_mappings.to: the same three verbs taking a single options object in camelCase: `send({messageId, recipient, payload, dedupKey, nowMs, epoch, runId})`, `poll(recipient, {nowMs, epoch, clock})`, `ack(messageId, {nowMs, recipient})`
systematic_mappings.why: The shape `src/control_plane/outbox.ts` already established for the same arguments, so the facade and the module it fronts are called the same way. JavaScript has no keyword arguments; an options object is the repository's settled substitute, and matching the outbox matters more here than anywhere because this class exists to be a thin skin over it. Systematic and therefore not repeated per case.
systematic_mappings.affects: every case that drives the bus

systematic_mappings.from: `@dataclass(frozen=True) DeliveredEnvelope` with snake_case fields, and `dataclasses.asdict(envelope)` at the wire
systematic_mappings.to: a frozen class with camelCase fields, and an explicit `envelopeToWire` in `endpoint.ts` that spells the snake_case wire keys out
systematic_mappings.why: The TypeScript surface is camelCase like the rest of the port, but the WIRE is not the API: `message_id` is the argument name the `ack` tool's own `inputSchema` declares, and an MCP client configured against interlock already parses those keys. So the rename stops at the transport boundary, and it is written out at that boundary rather than falling out of a serializer -- a serializer would make the wire contract a side effect of a naming convention.
systematic_mappings.affects: the envelope and the endpoint's two tool payloads

systematic_mappings.from: `pytest.raises(ValueError)` -- Python spells both the outbox's usage errors and the bus's own recipient-boundary refusal as the one builtin
systematic_mappings.to: `expectRefusal(..., OutboxUsageError)` for the outbox's, and `expectRefusal(..., MessageBusUsageError)` for the bus's own
systematic_mappings.why: `docs/test-translation-conventions.md` records why `expectRefusal` asserts the class as well as the message: a refusal family whose members differ only by message stays green while the taxonomy a caller acts on is wrong. Python collapses these two into `ValueError` because that is the builtin available; keeping them collapsed here would mean an ack refused by the WRONG layer still passed the test. The outbox's own refusals keep reaching callers unchanged, which is the source's stated 'exceptions are the outbox's own' doctrine.
systematic_mappings.affects: the two ack-refusal cases and the endpoint's tool-error case

systematic_mappings.to: `busEnv()` / `busEnvFactory()` in `test/messagebus/_env.ts`, called from the test body, with the source's `yield`-teardown becoming `onTestFinished`
systematic_mappings.why: Vitest has no `conftest.py`, so the source's split between the module that knows the control plane and the conftest that exposes it as fixtures has nothing to sit on and the two are merged. The property that split existed to produce -- no single file in the suite knows both the control plane and a session backend -- is unchanged and is still checked file by file by `import-graph.test.ts`. `onTestFinished` rather than an `afterEach` because it runs on failure too: a database left open by a failing case leaks a handle into whatever runs next, and under `sequence.shuffle` (D-0005) that is a different case each run.

target_only_tests.note:
Five cases, none of them ported coverage, and the source could not have carried them: interlock's bus at 65f36c5 runs on an outbox whose only terminal status is `acked`, so there is no `cancelled` for a poll to race against and nothing to translate. The status arrived here with migration `0003_outbox_cancelled_status.sql`, which makes `pending -> cancelled` and `delivered -> cancelled` legal edges and gives `cancelled` no outgoing edge at all (`src/control_plane/outbox.ts:190`, `TERMINAL_OUTBOX_STATUSES`); gate closure takes those edges from `src/control_plane/gates.ts:1661` without consulting this bus, so the writer that ends a relay is not the writer polling it. WHAT THE FOUR PIN, taken together, is one claim: a cancellation that lands mid-poll is a NORMAL FINISH and not a failure. `MessageBus.poll` decides terminality twice -- the post-snapshot re-read at `src/messagebus/bus.ts:265` and the post-exception residual test at `:351` -- and until this change both asked only whether the row was `acked`. Both now ask `isTerminalOutboxStatus`, so a fifth status added to 0003's CHECK is classified in one place rather than missed in this package. The window is not narrow and cannot be closed by checking first: `Outbox.due` reads a list ONCE and `poll` then walks it one attempt at a time, so every row after the first is attempted against a database that may have moved, and the gate is a separate writer whose write can land inside `attempt()` itself. The blast radius is what makes this worth four cases rather than one assertion: the re-read site falling through would run the destination side effect and then have `_MARK_DELIVERED` aborted by the forward-only trigger -- the effect happens and the database denies it ever did -- while the residual site re-throwing leaves `poll` entirely, discarding every envelope already built in that batch (the array is local and never returned) and surfacing to the worker as an `isError` tool response. One relay whose human gate closed must not fail a poll carrying this recipient's other work. The five split by window rather than by assertion: cancelled before the send is ever polled; cancelled after delivery, so a late ack must be a no-op rather than a refusal; cancelled between the `due()` snapshot and the attempt, which the re-read catches; cancelled from inside the attempt at `before_durable_write`, where the fenced statement itself misses its row; and cancelled from inside the attempt one checkpoint later, at `after_record_before_effect`, where the fenced write has already committed and only a guard standing immediately in front of `handler.apply` can still stop the effect. Those last three are separated on purpose, because they are three DIFFERENT sites and each is the only case covering its own. WHY THESE SITES NEED THEIR OWN WARRANT: `docs/design/minimal-operating-loop.md` section 5.1 enumerates four SQL predicates to align and says at line 694 to treat them "as the floor rather than the list". Neither of these two sites is on that list, and the reason is structural rather than an oversight anyone should repeat -- they live in `src/messagebus/bus.ts`, written in TypeScript against `load().status`, so a search of the outbox's SQL does not find them. These cases are the part above the floor, written down here so the next reader of 5.1 does not conclude the four predicates were the whole job.

THE FIFTH CASE ARRIVED IN ROUND 2 OF THIS BELT'S REVIEW, and it is registered separately because it pins TWO lines that are only ever correct together. `Outbox.attempt` now re-reads the row's status immediately before `handler.apply`, beside the fence re-read and for the same reason -- the top-of-method terminal check answered `was this message finished when I picked it up`, and since 0003 that is a different question from `is it finished now` -- and when that re-read finds a terminal row it records a durable refusal and throws `CancelledBeforeEffect` WITH THE EFFECT NOT YET PERFORMED. `MessageBus.poll` then admits that class alongside `OutboxUsageError` and `StaleWriterRefused` in the post-exception residual test, so the throw ends ONE MESSAGE rather than the poll. `a cancellation just before the effect costs one message, not the batch` drives a two-message poll, cancels the first at `after_record_before_effect`, and asserts the surviving batch as one equality over the whole result (`["task-2"]`, so a poll returning both fails as loudly as a poll returning neither) plus the destination's own effect count for the cancelled one. Each half of the fix has its own red: delete the widening in `bus.ts` and the throw leaves `poll` entirely, discarding every envelope already built in that local array -- including one whose effect has really happened -- and surfacing to the worker as an `isError` tool response; delete the guard in `attempt` and nothing throws at all, the side effect fires for a message whose gate has closed, and `_MARK_DELIVERED`'s `status = 'pending'` conjunct then matches no cancelled row, so the effect happened and the control plane denies it ever did. The destination's ledger is the only witness that separates those two worlds, because the outbox row looks identical in both -- which is exactly what made the missing guard survivable without this case.

entries.reason: Same assertion -- with a live clock the attempt past the lease expiry is refused loudly and the second row is left `pending`, so the fence holds through the poll rather than only at its first row. Adapted because the clock stub had to gain a failure the source got for free: `iter([...])` plus `next()` raises `StopIteration` on a third read, and a JavaScript closure over an array would silently return `undefined` and hand the outbox a `NaN` instant. The stub therefore throws an explicit error naming the third read, which keeps 'this case describes exactly two attempts' an assertion instead of an assumption.
